newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-Foreign firms compete for Indian consumer.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Foreign firms compete for Indian consumer.

text.p: Samir Verma of advertising firm Ammiratis Puris Lintas, thinks Reebok International Ltd must be mad to try selling its shoes in India at global prices.
"This company must be crazy. I'd wear 4,000 rupee ($112) shoes only on my head," the general manager says, shaking his head.

A good pair of Indian sneakers can cost as little as 500 rupees, and Verma is not the only one in shock: So are marketing officials at foreign consumer goods firms, whose mouths once watered greedily at the thought of grabbing a chunk of one of the world's largest markets.
"We never thought it would be so complicated," said a senior marketing official at one multinational company. "The Indian consumer is a difficult creature to understand."
Advertising agencies, waiting to catch multinationals rushing into India, say most ignore the pitfalls of selling in a nation as large as much of Europe -- and a great deal poorer.
INDIAN CONSUMERS EXTREMELY PRICE-SENSITIVE
The fundamental mistake most firms make is to treat pricing like a sacred cow, said Sandeep Goyal, executive vice president of advertising agency Rediffusion-Dentsu, Young and Rubicam.

"The sort of classic mistake that people make is to say: I won't sell it for less than my world price," Goyal said. "When you come in with a dollar-denominated price, you will only get dollar-denominated volumes."
"You shouldn't be wonderstruck and say 'But we didn't get the volumes'. You won't get the volumes. There are only so many volumes at that price."
Part of the problem is that Indian consumers are extraordinarily price-sensitive, Verma said.

"In terms of price-value equations, Indians are willing to pay less for quality than other markets and other countries," he said. "People are not willing to pay more than five or 10 percent extra for excellent quality and service."
Goyal said companies like Coca-Cola Co and Pepsico Inc had caught on fast, pricing their soft drinks at just seven rupees a bottle compared to the dollar equivalent of about 35 rupees abroad.
"The soft drink guys are one example -- they're looking at genuinely expanding the market, they're getting people to switch from traditional drinks," he said.
"The guys who are making substantial progress are those companies who have come in and figured out -- you want to sell in India, you've got to sell at Indian prices."
FAMOUS BRAND NAMES HAVE NO ASSURED CUSTOMERS
Goyal said many foreign firms take the consumer for granted.

"Just the fact that you're General Motors or Ford is not nearly enough reason to buy your product. When large international majors come into this country, they take the fact that they're a well known brand at face value and figure that they don't need to sell their credentials," he said.

He said another mistake many firms make is trying to sell globally unpopular goods to Indians, thinking that they will be absorbed by a market that for decades has had access to only Indian consumer goods due to strict import curbs.
"So you bring your worst products from abroad," Goyal said. "They won't buy it, Indians are quite smart. Just because it's a low-cost economy doesn't mean you can sell inferior products."
MYTH OF THE MIDDLE CLASS
Verma said many multinational companies, lured by the size of the market, rush into India with blinkers on.
"One of the fundamental problems they face is that everybody's looked at this huge number of 250 million middle class consumers," Verma said.
"Actually, it's a myth. It's the same minuscule lot that's buying everything. Only six percent of the Indian population has the propensity to get into the premium segment."

"It's not just a vast, homogeneous, amorphous mass of consumers," he said, referring to an array of ethnic groups scattered across the sprawling nation, where three-fourths of the 950 million people live in villages.
Verma said one U.S.-based food company was struggling to sell its cereals in India because it had underestimated the tradition-bound eating habits of the Indian consumer.
"To change the morning eating habit is a very, very difficult thing to do -- it's the most difficult habit to break after the morning paper," Verma said.

Fast food chain McDonalds Corp, on the other hand, was a success because it pushed its outlets as family restaurants. "That is an Indian thing," Verma said. "People go even to a fast food joint as a family outing."
SELLING IN INDIA AN EXPENSIVE PROPOSITION
Goyal said retailing in India slaps unexpected costs onto a firm's operations because sales are typically made through several small shops scattered across a city, rather than a supermarket.

"That means to service 100 units which could have happily gone into one supermarket, you have to cover 25 shops," he said. "Your feet on the street go up because you now require 25 salesmen opposed to one. The cost of operations keeps going up."
Verma agreed. "It's a funny country," he said. "The first thing you should do is do your homework very, very carefully." ($1 = 35.7 rupees)
